Shell Argument Assembly

An entry in the community catalog of software weakness descriptions.

Entry 78: Shell Argument Assembly

Description
The product assembles a command string from values a caller supplies and hands the result to a system shell, so the caller can steer what the shell actually runs. See the parent entry for the general form of the problem.

A shell reads its argument string before running anything, and every character it treats as punctuation is a chance for a caller to end one command and begin another.

The weakness appears whenever a value that crossed a trust boundary is concatenated into a string that will later be interpreted rather than merely stored.

Whether the value arrives from a form field, a header, a queue message or a file name makes no difference to the outcome; only the interpretation step matters.

Products that build their command strings once and reuse them are affected exactly as much as products that rebuild them per request.

Escaping the value is a narrow repair, because the correct escaping rules depend on which shell reads the string and on how that shell was invoked.

Passing an argument vector to the operating system directly, with no shell in between, removes the interpretation step and with it the weakness.

Common Consequences

A caller who controls part of the command string generally gains the privileges of the process that runs the shell, which is often broader than the feature required.

Where the process holds credentials for a downstream system, those credentials become reachable as well, so the blast radius is rarely limited to the affected host.

Recovery is expensive because the surviving evidence is a shell history rather than an application log, and the two are rarely correlated.

Demonstrative Examples

The listing below builds a directory listing command from a request parameter and executes it through the shell, which is enough to reproduce the weakness.

(bad code)
Example Language: PHP
$account = $_GET["account"];
$listing = 'ls -l /srv/accounts/' . $account;
shell_exec($listing);

The parameter is placed into the string without any check on what it contains, so a caller who appends a separator gets a second command executed under the same account.

Rewriting the same routine to call the directory listing facility of the language, with the account name passed as a separate argument, removes the shell entirely.

Applicable Platforms
Languages
Server-side scripting runtimes and shell wrappers

Reported often in code that shells out to platform utilities
